subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: Chinmay, come here, and I, Saurabh, will tell you how I got my first remote-control car. I was ten. It cost Rs 600 and I got Rs 50 a week. I sat with a pencil and thought aloud: 600 divided by 50 is twelve. Twelve weeks! At first that sounded forever. But then I counted twelve Sundays on the calendar, and I could see it. It was a number, not a mountain. If I skipped the ice-cream stall on some Fridays, it might even be less. So I decided: keep going, one Sunday at a time. On the twelfth Sunday I bought the car myself, and I never let it out of my sight.

qa.q: How much money did Saurabh get each week?
Why did Saurabh decide to keep going after working out twelve weeks?
qa.a: Saurabh saw twelve weeks as a number that could be counted and reached, and felt the goal was possible instead of impossible.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have made the wait shorter, and why?
qa.a: Skipping the ice-cream stall on some Fridays could shorten the wait, because money not spent adds to the savings each week.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the story as the listener?
qa.a: Chinmay is being told how a big price became twelve steps, so it probably shows that a long wait can feel smaller when it is broken into weeks.

grounding: A boy divides the toy's price by weekly pocket money to get twelve weeks and decides to continue because the number seems reachable.

subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: The red remote-control car in the shop window cost Rs 600, and Thomas had nothing saved. His elder brother Yogesh laughed. "Six hundred? On your pocket money? Forget it." It was raining, and they were sheltering under the shop's awning, waiting for the bus. Thomas pressed his nose to the glass and did the sum in his head. Fifty rupees every Saturday. Fifty, a hundred, a hundred and fifty... too slow to count. Then he tried dividing. 600 divided by 50. Twelve. Twelve Saturdays. "That's only three months," he said aloud. "Before my birthday, even." Yogesh stopped laughing. Thomas took one last look at the car and got on the bus, already counting.

qa.q: How much does Thomas get each Saturday?
How did Thomas feel once he worked out twelve Saturdays?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and determined, because twelve Saturdays, about three months, seemed reachable.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do to stay on track?
qa.a: Mark the twelve Saturdays on a calendar and share his plan with his parents; dividing the price made the goal feel possible.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Thomas's plan after the sum?
qa.a: Yogesh stops laughing, so he seems surprised the goal is more reachable than he thought.

grounding: Shows a boy dividing a Rs 600 toy car's price by his Rs 50 weekly pocket money, getting twelve weeks, and deciding it is reachable.

subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
passage: At his friend's birthday in their Chennai colony, Lalit had driven a remote-control car around the living room for ten whole minutes. Back home, he asked Appa how much one cost. "About Rs 600." Lalit sat at the dining table with a notebook, his sister Simran peering over. "I get Rs 50 every Sunday. So..." He wrote 600 ÷ 50 and worked it out slowly. "Twelve. Twelve Sundays." Simran counted on her fingers. "That's till the end of March." Lalit tapped the pencil. Twelve didn't sound like forever. Twelve was the number of chapters in his science book, and he'd finished those. "Okay," he said. "I'm doing it." He drew twelve boxes on the page.

qa.q: What did Lalit draw on the page?
Why did twelve not seem like forever to Lalit?
qa.a: He felt confident, comparing it to the twelve science chapters he had already finished, so the goal seemed reachable.

qa.q: What else could Lalit talk over with Appa?
qa.a: Where to keep the money safe each Sunday and whether the price might change; working out twelve weeks gave him a clear goal.

qa.q: How does Simran see Lalit's plan?
qa.a: Simran helps count to the end of March, so she seems interested and supportive.

grounding: Illustrates a boy dividing a Rs 600 toy's price by his Rs 50 a week, finding twelve weeks, and deciding the goal is reachable.
